**Video:** [Lec 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models : LLMs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=41tyjrCeENA)

## Learning goals

- Frame an LLM as a **next-token** generative model over text.
- Sketch why **transformers** (attention) scale to long context.
- Distinguish **pretraining**, **finetuning**, and **prompting** at an intro level.

## Before this clicks

Text is a sequence of tokens $w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T$ (subword pieces). A language model assigns probability

$$
p(w_1,\ldots,w_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
$$

Training on huge corpora to predict the next token teaches syntax, facts, and many skills as a side effect of compression / prediction. “Large” refers to scale: parameters, data, and compute.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Next-token prediction

At each step the model outputs a softmax over the vocabulary. Loss is cross-entropy of the true next token (maximum likelihood for the autoregressive factorization). Generation: sample or greedily pick $\hat w_t$, append, repeat.

### 2. Transformers (intuition)

Instead of processing tokens only left-to-right with a recurrent hidden state, **self-attention** lets each position form a weighted mix of other positions’ representations:

$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V
$$

(schematic). Stacked attention + feed-forward blocks yield deep contextual embeddings. Positional information is added so order matters.

### 3. Pretrain $\to$ adapt

| Stage | What happens |
|-------|----------------|
| **Pretrain** | Next-token (or related) loss on broad unlabeled text |
| **Finetune** | Continue training on a narrower labeled / instruction dataset |
| **Prompt** | Freeze weights; steer behavior with carefully chosen input text (and optional few-shot examples) |

Instruction tuning and RLHF-style preference optimization are common post-pretrain stages in modern chat models — course-level: adaptation need not always mean full retraining from scratch.

### 4. Capabilities and limits (honest intro)

- Strengths: fluent text, translation-ish behavior, coding assist, tool use when wrapped in systems.
- Limits: hallucinations (fluent wrong answers), context-window bounds, sensitivity to prompt wording, cost/latency, data bias.

### 5. Link to the course

LLMs are **generative sequence models**. Attention is a learned similarity-weighted combination — kin in spirit to kernels / soft lookup, but trained end-to-end at scale. Prompting is inference-time control of a conditional generative model $p(w\mid\mathrm{context})$.

---

## Worked mini-example

Context: “The capital of France is”. The model’s next-token distribution should put high mass on “Paris”. Pretraining saw many such patterns; no explicit geography database is required for that particular fact to appear — but the same mechanism can invent plausible-sounding errors, which is why verification matters.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| LLM = search engine | It **generates** tokens from $p(w_t\mid\mathrm{past})$, not retrieve-by-default. |
| Prompting trains the model | Ordinary prompting does **not** update weights. |
| Bigger always true | Scale helps many benchmarks; it does not guarantee factuality. |

1. Write the autoregressive factorization of $p(w_1,\ldots,w_T)$.
2. What loss is used for next-token pretraining?
3. What mechanism lets transformers mix information across positions?
4. Difference between finetuning and prompting?
5. Name one failure mode of LLMs despite fluent output.
